3 DISCUSSION
4 The first issue before the Court is whether Defendant knowingly, intelligently, and
s voluntarily waived his Miranda rights. Defendant argues that Detective Nucum exploited
6 Defendant's vulnerable state by choosing to mirandize and question him despite·knowing that he
7 had been banging his head in the cell, was in pain, and needed medical attention. (Mot. Suppress
8 at 8).
9 The Fifth Amendment of the United States Constitution provides that "[n]o person ...
10 shall be compelled in any criminal case to be a witness against himself," U.S. Const. amend. V,
11 and is applicable to Guam through the Organic Act. See 48 U.S.C.A. § 1421b(d). "The main
12 purpose of Miranda is to ensure that an accused is advised of and understands the right to remain
13 silent and the right to counsel." Berghuis v. Thompkins, 560 U.S. 370, 383 (2010). The burden
is on the Government "to demonstrate that Defendant knowingly and intelligently waived his
14
15 privilege against self-incrimination and his right to retained or appointed counsel." Miranda v.
16 Arizona, 384 U.S. 436,475 (1966).
11 "The voluntary, knowing and intelligent nature of a Miranda waiver is to be gleaned from
18 the totality of the circumstances, and the People bear the burden of proving by a preponderance
19 of the evidence that the waiver was properly made. A court reviewing such a waiver must
20 examine the entire record and make an independent determination of the ultimate issue of
21 voluntariness based on the totality of circumstances." People v. Towai, 2024 Guam 9 ,r 33
,r
22 (internal citations omitted). See also People v. Perez, 2021 Guam 18 19 ("Our jurisprudence
23 on waivers of constitutional rights considers the totality of the circumstances surrounding a
24 waiver, including a defendant's language abilities, coercive circumstances, awareness of the
25 relevant and likely circumstances, and knowledge of the right being abandoned.").
26 Here, although Defendant was diagnosed with methamphetamine intoxication and had
27 recently been banging his head against the holding cell cage (resulting in a visible abrasion on his
28 forehead), he was nevertheless found to be alert, oriented and responsive both at the precinct and
People v. Tedtaotao

Page 5 of7

at GRMC. "The physical injuries or medical treatment must affect a defendant's ability to
2 intelligently decide whether to waive his rights before such circumstances will require
3 suppression of statements." State v. Pinela, 458 N.W.2d 795, 797 (S.D. 1990). The evidence
4 does not support such an effect here. Despite the forehead abrasion and his report of right sided
5 rib pain, Defendant's cognitive functioning remained intact to a degree sufficient to understand
6 his rights and voluntarily interact with officers. Defendant read aloud, initialed, signed, and
7 confirmed understanding of each Miranda right. His intoxication was clinically mild; he was
8 oriented and communicative. Further, the brief interval between Defendant's request for medical
9 assistance and the administration of Miranda warnings does not, by itself, render the waiver
10 involuntary. Detective Nucum did not condition medical treatment on cooperation. When
II medical personnel arrived roughly ten minutes later, questioning ceased, and no evidence was
12 presented showing the medical care was delayed or obstructed. Accordingly, the Court finds no
13 basis to grant the Motion to Suppress on this ground.
14 The Court next turns to whether or not Defendant's statement was involuntary or coerced.
15 Defendant argues he was coerced into writing his statement because officers threatened to arrest
16 his girlfriend, Ms. Cruz, if he did not provide a statement, and because Detective Nucum dictated
17 what he should write. (Mot. Suppress at 8). "Involuntary or coerced confessions are inadmissible
18 at trial, because their admission is a violation of a defendant's right to due process under the
19 Fourteenth Amendment. A confession is involuntary if it is not 'the product of a rational intellect
20 and a free will."' Brown v. Hore!!, 644 F.3d 969,979 (9th Cir. 2011) (internal citations omitted).
21 "[C]oercive police activity is a necessary predicate to the finding that a confession is not
22 'voluntary' within the meaning of the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment."
23 Colorado v. Connelly, 479 U.S. 157, 167 (1986).
24 Coercive police activity can be the result of either physical intimidation or
psychological pressure. Whether a confession is involuntary must be analyzed
25
within the totality of the circumstances. The factors to be considered include the
26 degree of police coercion; the length, location and continuity of the interrogation;
and the defendant's maturity, education, physical condition, mental health, and age.
27
Brown, 644 F.3d at 979 (internal citations and quotation marks omitted).
28
People v. Tedtaotao
Case No. CF03 l 6-25
Decision and Order

In this case, the Court finds that Defendant's concern for Ms. Cruz during the interview
2 does not amount to coercion absent credible evidence that officers exploited that concern. No
3 threats, promises, or coercion were credibly established. There was no testimony that Defendant's
4 demeanor changed throughout the interview. The interview was approximately ten minutes long
5 and as noted earlier, Defendant was alert, oriented and communicative. Further, Defendant
6 acknowledged that the incriminating details provided during the oral interview came from him
7 and that the written statement as drafted and signed by him. Therefore, the Court finds that
8 Defendant's statement was the product of a rational intellect and a free will, and denies
9 Defendant's Motion to Suppress.
10 CONCLUSION
11 For the foregoing reasons, the Court hereby DENIES Defendant's Motion to Suppress.
